cards.title: ConfigMap — Non-Sensitive Configuration
cards.teaser: A ConfigMap stores arbitrary key-value pairs or file content that pods consume as environment variables or mounted files. It exists to decouple configuration from the container image, so the same image runs in dev, staging, and production with different settings.

runs.text: is a Kubernetes object that holds non-sensitive configuration data as key-value pairs. Values can be short strings (a database hostname, a feature flag) or entire file contents (an nginx.conf, a JSON properties file).
A minimal ConfigMap that supplies two configuration values:
field holds UTF-8 content. Binary content belongs in the
field as base64. A single ConfigMap can mix short string values and multi-line file bodies.
. They are stored in etcd in plain text, are visible with
to anyone with read access, and can be accidentally logged. Passwords, tokens, and certificates belong in a Secret, not a ConfigMap.
The 12-factor app principle III ("Config") states that config must be separated from code. ConfigMaps are Kubernetes's direct implementation of that principle for non-sensitive settings.
A ConfigMap is a named bag of settings you attach to pods at runtime so the same container image can behave differently in dev versus production without rebuilding.

cards.title: Secret — Sensitive Data (and the Base64 Misconception)
cards.teaser: A Secret holds sensitive data like passwords, tokens, and TLS certificates. The critical misconception is that base64 encoding is encryption — it is not. Without additional controls, a Secret is essentially a ConfigMap with a warning label.

runs.text: stores sensitive data. Kubernetes base64-encodes the values, but base64 is an encoding scheme, not an encryption scheme. Anyone who can run
has the plaintext value in under two seconds.

Base64 is NOT encryption. By default, Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd. Anyone with direct etcd access or sufficient RBAC permissions to read Secrets can recover the original value instantly. Treat a Secret as confidential at rest only when you have configured encryption providers (see the KMS card in this chapter).
The equivalent manifest (values must be manually base64-encoded in YAML):

explanation.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
type: Opaque
data:
  DB_PASSWORD: czNjcjN0   # base64 of "s3cr3t"
  DB_USER: YXBwdXNlcg==   # base64 of "appuser"

runs.text: for service account tokens. These types allow Kubernetes components to handle the Secret appropriately.

A Secret is a ConfigMap that Kubernetes marks as sensitive and base64-encodes — but base64 is reversible by anyone with access, so a Secret is only truly protected when you add encryption at rest and tight RBAC.

cards.title: envFrom — Bulk Injection as Environment Variables
cards.teaser: envFrom injects every key in a ConfigMap or Secret as a separate environment variable in one declaration, eliminating the need to enumerate each key individually. Convenient for large configs, but it can silently introduce unexpected variable names.

runs.text: When a ConfigMap or Secret has many keys, listing each one with

explanation.text:
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:1.0
    envFrom:
    - configMapRef:
        name: app-config          # all keys become env vars
    - secretRef:
        name: db-credentials      # all keys become env vars
      prefix: DB_                 # optional: prepend a prefix to avoid collisions

runs.text: With the configuration above, every key in
) is visible in the container's environment.

items.text: if the ConfigMap or Secret is updated, the pod must be restarted to pick up the new values — environment variables are captured at container startup.
keys that are not valid shell variable names (e.g., containing hyphens) are silently skipped. This can cause surprising missing-variable bugs.
Keys from multiple sources can collide.
When two sources define the same key, the last one listed wins. Use the
field to namespace keys from different sources.

runs.text: envFrom is a shortcut that dumps every key from a ConfigMap or Secret into the container's environment at once, instead of mapping each key manually.

cards.title: valueFrom — Selective Environment Variable Injection
cards.teaser: valueFrom maps a specific ConfigMap or Secret key to a named environment variable in the container. It gives you precise control over which keys are exposed and what names they appear under, avoiding the accidental leakage of every key in envFrom.

runs.text: When you need only certain keys, or need to rename them inside the container,

explanation.text:
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:1.0
    env:
    - name: LOG_LEVEL               # name inside container
      valueFrom:
        configMapKeyRef:
          name: app-config          # ConfigMap name
          key: LOG_LEVEL            # key inside the ConfigMap
    - name: DATABASE_PASSWORD       # rename for clarity
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-credentials
          key: DB_PASSWORD
          optional: false           # fail pod startup if key is missing

runs.text: field (the default) causes the pod to enter
if the referenced key does not exist, surfacing the misconfiguration immediately. Setting
allows the container to start with an empty value — useful for feature-flag secrets that may not yet be provisioned.
You can also expose the pod's own metadata — name, namespace, resource limits — using
. This is the Downward API — the same injection mechanism, applied to cluster metadata rather than ConfigMaps or Secrets.
valueFrom maps one ConfigMap or Secret key to one environment variable with a specific name — precision injection rather than the bulk dump of envFrom.

cards.title: Volume Mounts for Configuration
cards.teaser: Mounting a ConfigMap or Secret as a volume makes each key available as a file inside the container. This is the right pattern for config files (nginx.conf, application.properties) and for secrets that applications expect to read from the filesystem rather than the environment.

runs.text: Environment variables work well for short scalar values. Large structured config files — nginx configuration, TLS certificates, application.yaml — are better delivered as mounted files. Every key in the ConfigMap or Secret becomes a file whose name is the key and whose content is the value.

explanation.text:
spec:
  volumes:
  - name: app-config-vol
    configMap:
      name: app-config
      items:                        # optional: select specific keys
      - key: nginx.conf
        path: nginx.conf            # filename inside the mount
  - name: tls-secret-vol
    secret:
      secretName: tls-certs
      defaultMode: 0400             # read-only for owner only
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:1.0
    volumeMounts:
    - name: app-config-vol
      mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d
      readOnly: true
    - name: tls-secret-vol
      mountPath: /etc/tls
      readOnly: true

items.text: when a ConfigMap is updated and mounted as a volume, Kubernetes automatically updates the files in the pod (typically within 1–2 minutes via the kubelet sync period). The application must re-read the file to pick up the change — not all apps support this.
also receive live updates when the Secret changes. This is critical for TLS certificate rotation.
controls Unix file permissions on the mounted files. Use
(owner read-only) for secrets to prevent other processes in the same pod from reading them.

runs.text: Unlike environment variables, volume-mounted config can be updated without restarting the pod. This makes volume mounts the preferred delivery mechanism for config that changes at runtime, including TLS certificates that rotate on a schedule.
Mounting a ConfigMap or Secret as a volume turns each key into a file the container can read — and unlike env vars, those files can be updated while the pod is running.

cards.title: Immutable ConfigMaps and Secrets
cards.teaser: Marking a ConfigMap or Secret as immutable disables the watch mechanism that monitors it for changes, reducing apiserver load significantly at scale. It also prevents accidental updates — a change requires deleting and recreating the object.

runs.text: Kubernetes continuously watches ConfigMaps and Secrets to detect changes and propagate them to pods. In a cluster with thousands of pods consuming hundreds of ConfigMaps, this watch traffic is substantial. The
field, stable since Kubernetes 1.21, opts a ConfigMap or Secret out of this watch entirely.

explanation.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config-v3
immutable: true
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "warn"
  MAX_CONNECTIONS: "100"

runs.text: flag itself also cannot be reverted to
. To update the config, create a new versioned ConfigMap (
) and update the pod spec to reference it.

items.text: the kubelet does not need to poll for changes, reducing apiserver load measurably at scale (hundreds of ConfigMaps consumed by thousands of pods).
prevents accidental in-place mutations. If config must change, a new named version is required — creating a natural audit trail.
immutable ConfigMaps pair well with versioned naming (
) — the same pattern Helm uses with chart revisions.

runs.text: Marking a ConfigMap or Secret immutable tells Kubernetes to stop watching it for changes — saving apiserver bandwidth and preventing accidental edits. To change it, you must create a new one.

cards.title: The 12-Factor Config Principle
cards.teaser: Factor III of the Heroku 12-Factor App manifesto says: store config in the environment, never in code. ConfigMaps and Secrets are Kubernetes's first-class implementation of this principle — the image is immutable; the environment is variable.

runs.text: Adam Wiggins and the Heroku team published the

as everything that varies between deployments (dev, staging, production): database URLs, service credentials, per-environment feature flags. The rule: config must be in the environment, not in the code.
The test for a 12-factor app: could you open-source the codebase right now without exposing any credentials? If not, the app is violating Factor III — config has leaked into the code.

items.text: hardcoded database URLs, checked-in .env files, environment names in if/else blocks. These create builds that cannot be promoted across environments without modification.
Anti-pattern — config files not in the environment:
a config file that varies per environment but is baked into the image at build time (e.g.,
). This couples the image to a specific environment.
build one image. Apply environment-specific ConfigMaps and Secrets at deploy time. The same image digest runs in every environment — only the attached configuration differs.

runs.text: (Factor IV — Backing Services): the URL and credentials for a database, cache, or queue must come from the environment, not from code, so that the backing service can be swapped without a rebuild.
The full methodology is at 12factor.net. Factors I (Codebase), III (Config), IV (Backing Services), and X (Dev/prod parity) are the most directly relevant to Kubernetes deployment patterns.

The 12-factor config rule is: build one image and inject everything that varies per environment — URLs, passwords, feature flags — at runtime via environment variables. ConfigMaps and Secrets are how Kubernetes enforces this.

cards.title: External Secrets Operator
cards.teaser: The External Secrets Operator (ESO) syncs secrets from external systems — HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager — into Kubernetes Secrets automatically. It keeps the source of truth outside the cluster and reduces secret sprawl.

runs.text: ) is a Kubernetes operator that reads secrets from external stores — HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, 1Password, and others — and creates or updates native Kubernetes Secrets. The cluster never becomes the source of truth for the secret value.

explanation.text:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h             # how often to re-sync
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secrets-manager
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: db-credentials          # Kubernetes Secret to create
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
  - secretKey: DB_PASSWORD        # key in the Kubernetes Secret
    remoteRef:
      key: prod/myapp/db          # path in AWS Secrets Manager
      property: password          # JSON field in the secret value

runs.text: (cluster-wide) defines how ESO authenticates to the external system. AWS integration typically uses IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA); Vault integration uses the Vault Kubernetes Auth method.

items.text: elapses, ESO re-fetches the value. If the external secret changed (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager rotated it), the Kubernetes Secret is updated automatically.
the cluster holds a synced copy; the authoritative value lives in Vault or Secrets Manager where access logging, versioning, and rotation policies are enforced.

runs.text: The External Secrets Operator watches your external secret store (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, etc.) and automatically creates the matching Kubernetes Secret — the cluster is always in sync without you manually copying secrets in.

cards.title: Sealed Secrets — Encrypted Secrets Safe for Git
cards.teaser: Bitnami Sealed Secrets encrypts a Kubernetes Secret into a SealedSecret resource that is safe to commit to a public git repository. Only the controller running in-cluster holds the private key to decrypt it.

runs.text: The GitOps workflow stores all cluster state in git. But a Kubernetes Secret manifest is base64-encoded plaintext — committing it to git means anyone with repository access has the secret.
(github.com/bitnami-labs/sealed-secrets) solves this by asymmetrically encrypting the secret value using the cluster's public key. Only the
running in the cluster can decrypt it.

items.text: namespace. It generates and manages a RSA key pair.
to git. The controller decrypts it and creates the underlying Kubernetes Secret.

explanation.text:
# Resulting SealedSecret — safe to commit
apiVersion: bitnami.com/v1alpha1
kind: SealedSecret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
  namespace: production
spec:
  encryptedData:
    DB_PASSWORD: AgBy8hL...   # RSA-OAEP encrypted ciphertext
    DB_USER: AgCT1kP...

runs.text: Sealed Secrets are scoped to a specific namespace and cluster by default. A sealed secret for the "production" namespace cannot be applied to "staging". Back up the controller's private key — losing it means all sealed secrets become permanently unrecoverable.
Sealed Secrets encrypts a Kubernetes Secret so you can safely check it into git. The cluster controller holds the private key and decrypts it on apply — nobody else can, even with the committed YAML.

cards.title: SOPS — Encrypted Files for Any Secret Backend
cards.teaser: Mozilla SOPS (Secrets OPerationS) encrypts specific values within YAML, JSON, or .env files using PGP, age, AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or Azure Key Vault. The file stays human-readable; only the values are encrypted. It decouples encryption from Kubernetes.

runs.text: (github.com/getsops/sops) encrypts individual values inside structured files. The keys remain in plaintext — the file retains its readable structure and can be diff'd in git — but the values are ciphertext. Decryption happens at deploy time using any supported KMS: PGP,
(preferred modern alternative to PGP), AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or Azure Key Vault.

explanation.text:
# .sops.yaml — encryption configuration
creation_rules:
- path_regex: secrets/.*\.yaml
  kms: arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789:key/mrk-abc123
  age: age1ql3z...   # local developer key

# After sops --encrypt secrets/db.yaml
DB_PASSWORD: ENC[AES256_GCM,data:aBcDeF...,tag:GhIjKl...,type:str]
DB_USER: ENC[AES256_GCM,data:mNoPqR...,tag:StUvWx...,type:str]
sops:
  kms:
  - arn: arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789:key/mrk-abc123
    created_at: '2024-01-15T10:00:00Z'
  lastmodified: '2024-01-15T10:00:00Z'

runs.text: SOPS integrates with Argo CD via
plugins, decrypting at render time without exposing the plaintext to the repository. Flux supports SOPS natively via

items.text: (github.com/FiloSottile/age) is the modern recommendation — simpler key management, no keyring daemon, designed for file encryption. PGP is supported for legacy compatibility.

SOPS encrypts the file's data key against multiple recipients (a CI KMS key + a developer's age key). Any one recipient can decrypt — enabling both CI pipelines and individual developers to work with the same encrypted file.

runs.text: SOPS encrypts only the values inside a YAML or JSON file, leaving keys readable — so you can track what secrets exist in git without exposing what they contain.

cards.title: Secret Rotation — Rolling Secrets Without Restarting Pods
cards.teaser: Secret rotation is the practice of periodically replacing credentials to limit the blast radius of a compromise. The challenge in Kubernetes is distributing the new value to running pods without causing downtime — a problem that envFrom (env vars) and volume mounts solve differently.

runs.text: Rotating a secret involves three distinct operations:
the old one. Kubernetes creates friction at the distribution step.

items.text: changes, running pods are unaffected — the env var was captured at container startup. A rolling restart (
) is required to pick up the new value.
Kubernetes updates the file on disk within the kubelet sync period (default 60s). Applications that watch the file (or reload on SIGHUP) can pick up the new secret without a pod restart.

the external system (database, API gateway) should accept both the old and new credentials during the rotation window to allow a graceful rollover. Only after all pods are confirmed to use the new credential should the old one be invalidated.

runs.text: When using the External Secrets Operator, rotation is straightforward: update the secret in the external store (AWS Secrets Manager rotates it on schedule), ESO syncs the new value to the Kubernetes Secret, and volume-mounted consumers pick it up automatically within the kubelet sync period.

Do not rely on pod restarts alone for rotation if high availability is required. A rolling restart of a large Deployment can take minutes — during which some pods run the old credential and some the new one. The external service must support concurrent validity or the rotation causes partial failures.

Rotating a secret means the old password is replaced with a new one. In Kubernetes, env-var-based secrets require a pod restart to pick up the change; volume-mounted secrets update on disk automatically — so rotation strategy depends on how you inject the secret.

cards.title: KMS-Backed Encryption at Rest
cards.teaser: By default, Kubernetes Secrets are stored as base64 plaintext in etcd. Encryption at rest — using an encryption provider backed by AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, or HashiCorp Vault — is the configuration that makes Secrets actually encrypted on disk.

runs.text: etcd is the backing store for all Kubernetes API objects, including Secrets. Without encryption at rest, anyone with filesystem or backup access to etcd can read every Secret in the cluster in plaintext (after reversing base64). Encryption at rest is configured in the kube-apiserver's

explanation.text:
# /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml (passed to kube-apiserver)
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources:
  - secrets
  providers:
  - kms:
      apiVersion: v2
      name: aws-kms-provider
      endpoint: unix:///var/run/kms-plugin/socket.sock
      cachesize: 1000
      timeout: 3s
  - identity: {}   # fallback: plaintext (for migrating existing objects)

runs.text: The encryption provider list is ordered: the first provider encrypts newly written Secrets; all providers are tried for decryption. The
provider (plaintext) must remain last during migration so that existing unencrypted Secrets can still be read. After running
kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -

items.text: the kube-apiserver generates a data encryption key (DEK) per Secret. The DEK is encrypted with a key encryption key (KEK) held in the external KMS. Only the DEK ciphertext is stored alongside the Secret in etcd — the KEK never leaves the KMS.

GKE enables etcd encryption at rest by default. EKS supports it via AWS KMS envelope encryption for the cluster's secrets. AKS supports it via Azure Key Vault. On self-managed clusters, you configure it explicitly.
every decryption of a KMS-backed Secret generates an API call to the KMS — giving you an audit trail of which workloads accessed which secrets, something base64 storage cannot provide.

runs.text: Enabling encryption at rest does not retroactively encrypt existing Secrets. You must trigger a re-write (kubectl replace) of all existing Secret objects after enabling the encryption provider for them to be encrypted on disk.

KMS-backed encryption at rest tells the apiserver to encrypt every Secret with a key held in an external key management service before writing it to etcd — so even raw etcd access yields ciphertext, not passwords.
